The authors revisit the problem of the growth of dense/cold gas in the cloud-crushing setup with radiative cooling.
The relative motion between the dense cloud and the diffuse medium produces a turbulent boundary layer of mixed gas with a short cooling time.
The Gronke-Oh criterion states that cold gas growth occurs when the cooling time of the mixed gas is shorter than the cloud-crushing time (t_cool,mix < t_cc).
The Li criterion states that growth occurs when the cooling time of the hot gas is shorter than 10 times the predicted cloud lifetime (t_cool,hot < 10 * t_life,pred).
The authors' simulations agree with the Gronke-Oh criterion and show cloud growth in the region between the Gronke-Oh and Li radii.
Clouds smaller than the Gronke-Oh radius are destroyed, while clouds larger than the Li radius also show dense mass growth at late times.
In the absence of cooling, the cold/dense cloud is mixed into the hot wind after a few cloud-crushing times.
With cooling, larger clouds (R_cl > R_GO) show an initial dip in dense mass followed by late-time growth as the mixed gas in the boundary layer cools and accretes onto the dense tail.
The authors perform higher resolution (R_cl/d_cell = 64) simulations with a smaller box size to better visualize the small-scale features of the turbulent wake.

The multiphase structure of the turbulent wake, with a broad range of temperatures and densities but in rough pressure balance, may help explain the ubiquity of the range of absorption/emission lines observed in various astrophysical sources.

The authors argue that radiative cloud-crushing simulations should be run long enough to allow for the late-time growth of the dense gas due to cooling of the mixed gas, but not so long that the background gas cools catastrophically.
The simulation domain should be large enough that the mixed gas is not lost through the boundaries.
While the mixing layer is roughly isobaric, the emissivity of the gas at different temperatures is fundamentally different from an isobaric single-phase steady cooling flow.
The authors choose parameters relevant to the circumgalactic medium (CGM), where recent observations have revealed the multiphase structure of the CGM.
Cold gas is also seen in cool core clusters, extended symmetrically out to the virial radius in z ≳ 3 halos hosting quasars, and within 10s of kpc in z ≳ 3 star-forming galaxies.
